passage: Supervisor's note, research lab Aparna, our new research assistant, is careful and very good at her work. But for three weeks she has arrived between forty minutes and an hour late. When I stayed late on Tuesday, I saw her check the gas taps on every bench, then go back and check them again, touching each one. She checked the lab door five times before leaving. When she saw me, she went red and said she'd forgotten her pen. What I did next: I asked her for a private chat, and said I wasn't there to blame her. She told me that if she doesn't check, she's terrified of a fire, and that it now takes hours every day. She'd hidden it from everyone. I gave her information about the staff health service and a qualified clinician they work with. We agreed a later start time for now. - Binita

qa.q: How many times did Aparna check the lab door before leaving?
qa.a: Five times.

qa.q: What does Aparna's excuse about the pen suggest she was feeling?
qa.a: It suggests she felt embarrassed and wanted to hide the checking from others.

qa.q: Which of Binita's choices made it easier for Aparna to open up?
qa.a: Binita spoke privately and made clear the chat wasn't about blame.

qa.q: How might Aparna's colleagues have seen her lateness without knowing the reason?
qa.a: They might have thought she was careless or not serious about her job, not that she was struggling with fear.

grounding: A supervisor sees a young adult spending hours checking, arriving late and hiding it, and points her to a qualified clinician.

passage: Saturday night Missed Pranav's birthday lunch today. Again. I told him the bus was late. It wasn't. The truth: I was home, arranging my books, spines lined up exactly, then checking the stove, then the books again because one looked tilted. Every time I finish, there's this sweet second of relief. Then the fear comes back louder, like it wants more. Two and a half hours today. Nobody knows. Not Pranav, not my flatmates. I tidy it up before they see. Tonight I looked at the university counselling page for a long time. They have a clinician who works with exactly this kind of thing. I've filled in the form. I haven't pressed send. Okay. Pressing it now. Tomorrow I'll tell Pranav the truth. - Leela

qa.q: How long did Leela spend arranging and checking today?
qa.a: Two and a half hours.

qa.q: How does Leela feel after each round of arranging, and what happens to the fear?
qa.a: There is a sweet second of relief, then the fear comes back louder, as if it wants more.

qa.q: What was the turning point at the end of the day?
qa.a: Leela pressed send on the university counselling form and decided to tell Pranav the truth.

qa.q: How might Pranav feel when Leela tells him why Leela missed the lunch?
qa.a: He may feel sorry Leela struggled alone and glad Leela trusted him with the truth.

grounding: It shows a young adult who spends hours arranging and checking, arrives late and hides it, feels brief relief that demands more, and seeks a qualified clinician.

passage:
Dear Ramesh bhaiya,
You asked why I missed your engagement lunch. I owe you the truth.
Every morning I spend nearly two hours checking the stove, the lock, the window latches, the plugs. Then I arrange my books by height and colour, and if one is wrong I start again. I've been late to lectures most of this term. I told my friends I had a stomach problem. They believe me.
The strange thing is, checking calms me for maybe a minute. Then the fear comes back bigger, and I need to check more.
I don't want to live like this. So yesterday I booked an appointment with a clinical psychologist at the university health centre. It's on Tuesday.
I'm sorry about the lunch. I really wanted to be there.
Abhinav

qa.q: How long does Abhinav spend checking each morning?
qa.a: Nearly two hours.

qa.q: How does Abhinav feel after checking?
qa.a: Abhinav feels calm for maybe a minute, then the fear comes back bigger, so checking brings only brief relief.

qa.q: What wise step has Abhinav taken?
qa.a: Abhinav booked an appointment with a clinical psychologist at the university health centre.

qa.q: How might Ramesh feel reading this letter?
qa.a: Ramesh may feel sad and worried but touched that Abhinav trusted Ramesh with the truth.

grounding: Shows a young adult spending hours checking and arranging, arriving late and hiding it from friends, whose relief is brief, and who wisely seeks a clinician.

passage: Remember our trip to Lonavala, Salma, when I kept you all waiting forty minutes at the bus stand? I said I'd lost my ticket. That wasn't true. I'd gone back to the flat three times to check the taps. At home my mother would say, "Usha, just leave it," and I'd nod and then check again. Every day I lined up my pens, my shoes, my plates until they felt right, sometimes for an hour. It made the scary feeling go away for a few minutes, and then it came back hungrier. I hid it from all of you because I was embarrassed. Last month I finally saw a clinical psychologist. We're working on it slowly. I wanted you to hear it from me.

qa.q: How long did Usha keep her friends waiting at the bus stand?
qa.a: Usha kept them waiting forty minutes.

qa.q: How did Usha feel after checking or arranging things?
qa.a: The scary feeling eased for a few minutes, but then came back stronger, and Usha felt embarrassed about hiding it.

qa.q: What did Usha finally do that was wise?
qa.a: Usha saw a clinical psychologist and is working on it slowly.

qa.q: How might Salma feel hearing the real reason for the delay?
qa.a: Salma may feel surprised and sympathetic, and glad that Usha trusted a friend enough to tell the truth.

grounding: Shows a young adult whose checking and arranging cause lateness that is hidden from friends, relief being brief, and who seeks a clinician.

passage:
Monday: Neelam, twenty, arrived at the college canteen an hour late. She had spent the morning arranging her hostel cupboard, taking everything out and putting it back until it felt right. "Traffic," she told Nilesh.
Wednesday: She missed the first half of a practical after checking her door lock eleven times. When Nilesh asked again, she snapped, "Why do you care?" Then she cried in the washroom. Each check calmed her for a moment and then demanded another.
Saturday: Neelam sat in the college clinic across from a clinical psychologist. "It's taking my whole day," she said. That evening she texted Nilesh: "Sorry for snapping. It wasn't traffic. Can I tell you what's going on?" He replied at once: "Of course. Coffee?"

qa.q: How many times did Neelam check her door lock on Wednesday?
qa.a: She checked it eleven times.

qa.q: How did Neelam feel when Nilesh asked again on Wednesday?
qa.a: She felt defensive and ashamed, snapping at him and then crying in the washroom.

qa.q: What steps did Neelam take on Saturday?
qa.a: She met a clinical psychologist at the college clinic and apologised to Nilesh, offering to tell him the truth.

qa.q: How might Nilesh feel reading Neelam's text?
qa.a: He may feel relieved and glad she trusts him, which is why he replies at once.

grounding: Shows a young adult losing hours to arranging and checking, arriving late and hiding it, whose relief is brief, and who seeks a qualified clinician.

passage:
You were late again, Vijay, and I saw you go back to check your scooter lock three times. So let me tell you something your Rajni Mausi has never told anyone in this family.
When I was twenty, in my college hostel, I began checking the iron was off. Once, then five times, then twenty. Then the taps, then the window latch. Each check gave me one sweet second of relief. Then the fear came back bigger, wanting more.
I missed my first class most days. My friends thought I was lazy. I told them I overslept. It was easier than the truth.
One day I stood at the door for an hour and cried. That evening I told my roommate, and the next week I saw a psychiatrist at the college hospital. It took a long time, beta, but it got smaller. So if this is you, don't hide it the way I did.

qa.q: How long did young Rajni stand at the door that day?
qa.a: An hour.

qa.q: How did young Rajni feel after each check?
qa.a: Young Rajni felt a brief second of relief, then the fear came back bigger, wanting more checks.

qa.q: What was the turning point in Rajni Mausi's story?
qa.a: Telling a roommate and seeing a psychiatrist at the college hospital, instead of hiding the checking from friends.

qa.q: How might young Rajni's friends have seen things back then?
qa.a: They thought Rajni was lazy and oversleeping, never guessing the fear being hidden.

grounding: Rajni Mausi tells Vijay how, at twenty, hours of checking caused lateness that was hidden from friends, with relief bringing more fear, until a qualified clinician was sought.
